title: Capstone 3: a typed printf with GADTs
body: A format description can compute the type of the function that uses it. With `type ('a, 'r) fmt = Lit : string -> ('r, 'r) fmt | Int : (int -> 'r, 'r) fmt | Str : (string -> 'r, 'r) fmt | Cat : ('a, 'b) fmt * ('b, 'r) fmt -> ('a, 'r) fmt`, the format `Cat (Lit "x=", Int)` has type `(int -> 'r, 'r) fmt`: printing with it needs exactly one `int`. Passing a string, or too few arguments, is a compile-time type error.

`'a` is the type of the printing function and `'r` is what it finally returns. A literal consumes nothing, so its two parameters are equal. `Int` consumes one int, so `'a` is `int -> 'r`. `Cat (f1, f2)` chains: `f1` turns `'a` into an intermediate `'b`, and `f2` turns that `'b` into `'r`, so the arguments of `f1` come before those of `f2`.

The interpreter is written in continuation-passing style, `kprintf : type a r. (string -> r) -> (a, r) fmt -> string -> a`, because each constructor changes the result type, which needs the explicit polymorphic annotation. `Lit` appends its text and calls the continuation. `Int` returns a function that waits for the int. `Cat` runs `f1` with a continuation that runs `f2`. This is the same idea as the standard library's `Printf`, in thirty lines.
challenge: In src/fmt.ml, `kprintf` only raises. Implement the four cases: `Lit s` calls `k (acc ^ s)`; `Int` and `Str` return a function that appends the converted argument and calls `k`; `Cat (f1, f2)` runs `f1` with a continuation that runs `f2` with the original `k`. `sprintf` is already `kprintf Fun.id f ""`.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. Edit only `kprintf` in src/fmt.ml. Try writing `sprintf (Cat (Lit "n=", Int)) "x"` in a scratch file and read the type error.
question: What does the type of `Cat (Lit "x=", Int)` tell you at compile time?
correct: That printing with it needs exactly one int argument, so a wrong argument is a type error
wrong: That it prints the letter x
That the format is checked only when it runs
reasoning: The GADT indexes the format by the function type it requires, so the type checker rejects mismatched arguments.
